title: Running the contract after award
summary: Award is the start, not the finish. Contract administration makes sure both sides do what the contract says: the contractor performs, the Government inspects, accepts and pays on time, and every change is handled properly and written down.
why: Administer Contract is 10 exam questions, and FAR Part 42 (Contract Administration and Audit Services) is on the exam list. Most of a contract's life happens after award.

sections.body:
- Hold a **post-award orientation conference** when the contract is complex or new to the contractor, so both sides understand roles, reports, inspection, invoicing and points of contact (listed among contract administration functions in FAR 42.302(a)(3)).
- Make sure the COR is designated in writing and trained, and that the contractor knows who the COR is and what the COR may and may not do.
- For some contracts, administration is delegated to a contract administration office, often the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA), which then acts through an administrative contracting officer (ACO) (FAR 42.2, 42.3).

A COR is designated in writing by the contracting officer, must be trained, and monitors technical performance, inspects and reports. A COR has **no authority** to change the contract's price, quantity, quality, delivery or other terms, or to direct the contractor to do new work (DFARS 201.404-70 and PGI). DoW CORs are appointed and tracked in the PIEE Joint Appointment Module.

- Invoices and receiving reports move electronically through **PIEE** (Wide Area WorkFlow).
- The Prompt Payment Act requires payment generally within 30 days after the Government receives a proper invoice or accepts the work, whichever is later. Late payments earn interest automatically, at a rate Treasury sets every six months (4.75% a year for July to December 2026) (FAR 32.9).
- On incrementally funded cost-type contracts, the Limitation of Funds clause (52.232-22) requires the contractor to warn the Government before funds run out.

- **Stop-work order:** the contracting officer can stop all or part of the work for up to 90 days, then cancel the order or terminate (FAR 42.10, 52.242-15).
- **Government property:** track property furnished to the contractor; the Government Property clause decides liability for loss or damage (FAR Part 45, 52.245-1(h)).
- **Novation and change-of-name agreements:** recognize a new contractor that bought the business, or a new company name (FAR 42.9).
- **Key personnel:** approve substitutions the contract requires you to approve.

Contracting officers evaluate contractor performance in the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS) during and at the end of contracts, generally those above the simplified acquisition threshold. The contractor gets a chance to comment, and future source selections use these records (FAR 42.11). Be fair, factual and specific.

example.title: The helpful COR
example.body: A COR tells the contractor to add a second shift 'just for this month.' The contractor does it and then asks to be paid. The COR had no authority: this may be a constructive change or an unauthorized commitment. The fix starts with the contracting officer, and the prevention starts at the post-award conference, where everyone hears that only the contracting officer changes the contract.

remember: CORs watch and report; they never change the contract.
Pay within 30 days of a proper invoice or acceptance, whichever is later, or interest is owed.
mistakes: Letting invoices sit, which costs the Government interest.
Writing vague CPARS comments that help no future buyer.

title: Quality: inspection, acceptance and warranties
summary: The Government checks that it gets what it paid for, then accepts it. Acceptance is usually final, so inspect before you accept, use the surveillance plan for services, and use warranties when they are worth it.
why: Ensure Quality is 10 exam questions, and FAR Part 46 (Quality Assurance) is on the exam list.

sections.body: The Government may inspect and test supplies and services at any reasonable time and place in the contract, at the source or at destination (FAR 46.4). For services, the COR follows the **quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP)**: what will be checked, how often and against which standards.

Nonconforming supplies or services can be:
- rejected, with the contractor required to correct or replace them, if time allows;
- accepted anyway, but only with a fair price reduction or other consideration when it is in the Government's interest.
Document every nonconformance; it supports cure notices, CPARS and, if needed, termination.

A warranty gives remedies after acceptance. It costs money, so weigh the nature and use of the item, cost, how the Government will enforce it, and trade practice (FAR 46.7). Commercial items usually come with the seller's standard warranty.

example.title: The hidden crack
example.body: Six months after acceptance, castings delivered under a supply contract crack in use. Testing shows an internal flaw that no reasonable inspection at delivery would have found. That is a latent defect, so the Government can still demand a remedy even though it accepted the castings.

remember: Inspect before you accept; acceptance is final except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or a warranty.
Services: the QASP says what, how and how often.
mistakes: Signing a receiving report before anyone checked the delivery.

title: Subcontracts
summary: The Government's contract is with the prime contractor only. The prime manages its subcontractors, but for some contracts the contracting officer must consent to certain subcontracts, and large businesses must meet their small business subcontracting plans.
why: Manage Subcontracts is 4 exam questions, and FAR Part 44 (Subcontracting Policies and Procedures) is on the exam list.

sections.body: The Government has privity of contract only with the prime. Subcontractors are the prime's responsibility: the Government does not direct them or pay them, and the prime cannot avoid its own obligations by blaming a subcontractor.

When the contract's Subcontracts clause requires it, the prime must get the contracting officer's **consent** before placing certain subcontracts, usually on cost-type, time-and-materials, labor-hour, letter or unpriced contracts, or when the prime's purchasing system is not approved (FAR 44.201-1). The contracting officer reviews things like competition, price analysis and the subcontract type (44.201-3). Consent does not make the Government a party to the subcontract or relieve the prime of responsibility. Some subcontracts need **advance notification** instead (44.201-2).

A contractor purchasing system review (CPSR), done by DCMA in DoW, evaluates how a large contractor spends Government money on subcontracts. An approved purchasing system reduces the need for consent (FAR 44.301).
Primes must pass certain clauses down to subcontractors (flowdowns). For commercial subcontracts, the required flowdowns are limited (FAR 44.4).

Large businesses winning contracts above the subcontracting plan threshold, when subcontracting opportunities exist, must have an approved small business subcontracting plan (FAR 19.109). They report progress in the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System (eSRS), and the contracting officer watches compliance.

example.title: The unpaid subcontractor
example.body: A subcontractor calls you: the prime has not paid it in 90 days and it wants the Government to pay directly. You cannot pay or direct the subcontractor, since there is no privity. You can remind the prime of its obligations, look at the prime's compliance with payment clauses, and record the issue in CPARS.

remember: Privity runs Government to prime, and prime to sub, never Government to sub.
Consent protects the Government; it does not take over the prime's responsibility.
mistakes: Giving technical direction to a subcontractor.
Treating consent as approval of every term of the subcontract.

title: Changes and modifications
summary: Only a contracting officer can change a contract, and only in writing with a modification. Some changes the contracting officer can make alone; others need the contractor's agreement. Every change that adds work needs funds and is priced through an equitable adjustment.
why: Manage Changes is 10 exam questions, and modifications will be a big part of your daily work.

sections.body: Only contracting officers acting within the scope of their authority may execute modifications. Other Government people must not direct or encourage the contractor to do work the contract does not require or to change the terms (FAR 43.202). Modifications are written on an SF 30.

- **Administrative change:** a unilateral change that does not affect the substance, such as a new paying office or corrected accounting data.
- **Change order:** a unilateral written order, under the Changes clause, directing a change within the general scope. The contractor must keep performing as changed (43.301(b)) and may ask for an equitable adjustment.
- **Supplemental agreement:** a bilateral modification signed by both parties, such as an agreed price for a change or a negotiated scope adjustment.
- **Exercising an option** is a unilateral modification by the Government.

In a fixed-price supply contract, the contracting officer may change drawings, designs or specifications, the method of shipment or packing, and the place of delivery, within the general scope (52.243-1). If the change affects cost or time, the contractor gets an **equitable adjustment** in price, schedule or both, and must assert its right to one within 30 days of receiving the order. Other contract types have their own Changes clauses (52.243-2 to 52.243-7).

- **Within scope:** something the original competitors could reasonably have expected under the contract.
- **Cardinal change:** a change so big it is outside the general scope. That is new work, which needs its own competition or justification.
- **Constructive change:** the Government, by words or actions rather than a formal order, makes the contractor do more or different work, for example a COR demanding extra work, or an unreasonable interpretation of the specifications. The contractor may be entitled to an adjustment.

No modification that adds cost may be issued without available funds (43.205). An option can be exercised only within its time limit, with written notice, when funds are available, the need still exists, the contractor is not excluded in SAM, performance has been acceptable, and exercising the option is the most advantageous way to meet the need given current prices (FAR 17.204-1(b)).

example.title: More gravel
example.body: A road project needs 20% more gravel because of soft ground. The contracting officer issues a change order within the general scope, telling the contractor to keep working, and certifies that funds are available. The contractor submits a proposal; you analyze it and negotiate a supplemental agreement for the equitable adjustment.

remember: Unilateral: administrative change, change order, option exercise. Bilateral: supplemental agreement.
Within scope = change order; outside scope = new procurement.
mistakes: Signing a change that adds cost before funds are certified.
Exercising an option late or without checking SAM and price.

title: Disputes and claims
summary: When the Government and a contractor cannot agree, the contractor can submit a claim. The contracting officer must issue a written final decision, and the contractor can appeal it to a board of contract appeals or the Court of Federal Claims. Strict deadlines apply on both sides.
why: Disputes sit in the Manage Changes and Manage Disagreements competencies, and the Contract Disputes Act numbers are favorite exam questions.

sections.body:
A **claim** is a written demand by one party asking, as a matter of right, for a sum of money, an adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief. A routine invoice is not a claim unless it is disputed and not paid in a reasonable time. Claims are governed by the Contract Disputes Act (41 U.S.C. 7101 to 7109) and FAR Subpart 33.2.

A contractor must submit a claim within **6 years** after it accrues.

Contractor claims over **$100,000** must be certified: made in good faith, supporting data accurate and complete, the amount accurate, and the person signing authorized to certify (FAR 33.205-2, clause 52.233-1(d)).

- For claims of $100,000 or less, decide within 60 days if the contractor asks for a decision in that time.
- For larger certified claims, within 60 days either decide or tell the contractor when a decision will be issued (FAR 33.205-6(c)).
- The decision is in writing, gives the reasons, and tells the contractor its appeal rights.
- If the contracting officer does not decide in time, the claim can be treated as denied, and the contractor may appeal.

- To the agency **board of contract appeals** (for DoW, the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals) within **90 days** of receiving the final decision; or
- to the **U.S. Court of Federal Claims** within **12 months**.
Interest on a successful claim runs from the date the contracting officer received it (FAR 33.205-3). While a dispute is open, the contractor must keep performing as directed (52.233-1).

Try to resolve disagreements at the contracting officer's level, using alternative dispute resolution (ADR) where it helps: mediation, facilitation, a minitrial, arbitration or an ombudsman, all voluntary (FAR 33.204). The Government can also have claims against a contractor, such as for defective pricing, and the contracting officer issues a final decision on those too.

example.title: The delay claim
example.body: A contractor submits a certified $420,000 claim for delays it says the Government caused. Within 60 days the contracting officer tells the contractor the decision will be issued in 120 days, after an audit. The final decision grants $150,000, explains why, and states the appeal rights: 90 days to the ASBCA or 12 months to the Court of Federal Claims.

remember: Over $100K: certify. Decide or set a date within 60 days.
Appeal: 90 days to the board, 12 months to the court. File a claim within 6 years.
mistakes: Treating a contractor's angry email as a claim without checking the definition.
Letting the contractor stop work because a dispute is pending.

title: Terminations
summary: The Government can end a contract for its convenience, paying for work done and a fair profit on it, or for default when the contractor fails to perform. Default terminations follow strict steps, usually a cure notice or a show cause notice first, and always legal review.
why: Terminations fall under Manage Changes, and FAR Part 49 (Termination of Contracts) is on the exam list.

sections.body: The Government may terminate all or part of a contract when it is in the Government's interest, for example when the need goes away (FAR Part 49, Subparts 49.2 and 49.3). The contractor stops work, protects property and submits a settlement proposal. It is paid its allowable costs for work done, a reasonable profit on that work (never on the terminated work), and reasonable settlement expenses (49.202). It does not get anticipated profit on the work it will no longer do.

The Government may terminate for default when the contractor (FAR 49.4):
- fails to deliver or perform on time;
- fails to make progress so that performance is endangered; or
- fails to perform other provisions of the contract.
Before terminating for the second or third reason, send a **cure notice** giving at least 10 days to fix the problem. When there is not enough time for that, or the delivery date has passed, a **show cause notice** asks the contractor to explain why it should not be terminated (49.402-3; sample notices at 49.607).

A contractor is not in default for delays beyond its control and without its fault, such as acts of God, fires, floods, epidemics, strikes or acts of the Government (52.249-14). After a proper default termination, the Government does not pay for unaccepted work and may charge the contractor the excess costs of buying the work from someone else (49.402-2). If a default termination is later found improper, it is converted to a termination for convenience.

Commercial contracts are terminated under the commercial terms clause (52.212-4), for convenience or for cause, not under the Part 49 procedures, although Part 49 can be used as guidance (FAR 12.304).

Consider alternatives: a no-cost cancellation if the contractor agrees, letting the contractor continue with a new schedule in exchange for consideration, or a mutual agreement. Get legal counsel involved, document everything, and remember a default termination is reported and affects the contractor's future.

example.title: Ten days to cure
example.body: A janitorial contractor misses cleaning in several buildings for three weeks despite COR reports. The contracting officer sends a cure notice: fix the failures within 10 days or face termination for default. The contractor brings in a new supervisor and performance recovers. Without the cure notice, a default termination for failure to perform would have been improper.

remember: Convenience: pay for work done plus profit on it. Default: cure (10 days) or show cause first.
mistakes: Terminating for default without a cure notice when one was required.
Paying profit on the terminated portion.

title: Closeout
summary: Closeout confirms everything is done and paid, sends unused money back, records the contractor's final performance, and closes the file within set time limits. Open files tie up funds the customer could have used.
why: Close Out Contract is 4 exam questions, and closeout backlogs are a common audit finding.

sections.h: When a contract is closed (FAR 4.308, Table 4-2)
sections.body:
Time limits start when the contracting officer receives evidence of physical completion:
- **Simplified acquisitions:** considered closed when the contracting officer has evidence of receipt and final payment, unless agency rules say otherwise.
- **Firm-fixed-price contracts** (other than simplified): within **6 months**.
- **Contracts that need indirect cost rates settled** (most cost-type): within **36 months**.
- **All other contracts:** within **20 months**.

A contract is physically complete when the contractor has delivered all supplies and performed all services and the Government has accepted them (or the contract was terminated), and all option periods have expired or no options remain.

example.title: Money left on the table
example.body: A firm-fixed-price contract finished in March still shows $22,000 obligated that will never be billed. Closing it out in time lets the customer reuse those funds while they are still available. Leaving it open for two years risks the funds canceling.

remember: FFP 6 months, indirect-rate contracts 36 months, all others 20 months.
Closeout gives money back: deobligate what will not be spent.
mistakes: Starting closeout only when an auditor asks.
